title: Nature & Geography Field Study
goal: Your kid picks one thing in the landscape where you're staying, like a volcano, a swamp, a reef or a mountain, and studies it like a field scientist. They ask one big why question, research it, go and see it for themselves, then explain what they found and how it shapes life here.
need: One landscape feature you can visit safely: a volcano, swamp, beach, forest or river
A park sign, guidebook or article that explains it
A notebook and a phone for photos
A local guide or ranger if you can find one

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: A great view can end the curiosity at 'wow'. Your job is to get one why question written down before you go, so the hike is about checking it. On the day, keep everyone on the marked trail, and beside you near edges, water and wildlife.

plan.when: When you know where you're going
plan.what: Spot the feature, ask the why, research it (Steps 1, 2 and 3).

troubleshoot.a: Ask what's different from home: the soil, the trees, the water, the weather. The ordinary local landscape is often the best study.

troubleshoot.q: The research is too hard to read
troubleshoot.a: Read it together and find one sentence that answers the question. A park sign or a ranger can often say it in plainer words.

troubleshoot.q: They lose interest on the hike
troubleshoot.a: Give them the evidence job: three photos that help answer the why. A job with a goal carries tired legs a long way.

lesson.text: A landscape is full of clues about how it was made. You read it by asking one good why question, finding out the answer, then going to see the evidence with your own eyes.
lesson.before: It's a big hole with green water.

model.line: Why is the water at the bottom of the crater so green?
The volcano sends up gases and sulfur, and the lake is very acidic.
We hiked to the rim and looked straight down at it.
The colour is a sign the volcano is still active.

lesson.modelNote: 'A hole with green water' described it. One why question, answered before the hike, turned the view from the rim into evidence.

steps.title: Spot the feature
steps.why: Picking one feature turns a whole landscape into something a kid can actually study.
steps.kid: Your kid looks at the landscape where you're staying and picks one feature to study, using the Read the landscape card in the Field Study Toolkit at the end of the guide: the land, the water, the plants, the animals or the weather. They choose the one that's most different from home.
steps.you: Help them see what's unusual here. Ask 'What do you see here that we don't have at home?' and list the options together.
ask: What's the biggest thing in this landscape?
What would surprise a friend from home?
steps.tip: Locals often point to the feature without being asked. Listen for what people here are proud of, or warn you about.

levels.explore: Pick one thing in the landscape that's different from home, and draw it.
levels.develop: Pick one feature, and say why it's worth studying.
levels.extend: Pick one feature, and find out how it was formed before you choose your question.

steps.title: Ask one big why
steps.why: One good question gives the whole study a direction.
steps.kid: Your kid writes one why question about the feature, using the Good why questions card, like 'Why is the water green?' or 'Why do these trees grow in water?' Then they write their best guess before looking anything up.
steps.you: Help them sharpen the question so it has a real answer. Write their guess down exactly as they say it, so they can check it later.
ask: What do you most want to know about it?
steps.tip: A guess written down first makes the research feel like checking a theory.

levels.explore: Ask one why question out loud, and say your guess.
levels.develop: Write one why question and a guess with a reason.
levels.extend: Write the question, a guess and what evidence would prove it right or wrong.

steps.title: Research it before you go
steps.why: Knowing what to look for is what makes it fieldwork.
steps.kid: Your kid finds the answer to their question from one or two sources: a park sign, a museum, a guidebook, an article or a local who knows. They compare it with their guess and list what to look for when they get there.
steps.you: Help them find a source that fits their reading level, and read it with them. Ask 'Was your guess right, partly right or wrong?'
ask: What will you look for when we get there?
steps.tip: Visitor centres, park signs and small local museums are made for exactly this, and they're usually right at the trailhead.

levels.explore: Listen to the answer read aloud, and say if your guess was right.
levels.develop: Find the answer in one source, and list two things to look for.
levels.extend: Check two sources, note anything they disagree on, and list three things to look for.

steps.title: See it for yourselves
steps.why: Seeing the evidence with your own eyes is what makes the answer stick.
steps.kid: Your kid visits the feature and collects evidence, using the Field notes card: photos, sketches, what they see, hear and smell. If there's a guide, they ask a question from the Ask the guide card.
steps.you: Book a guide where it makes sense, and stay on marked trails. Keep them beside you near edges, water and wildlife. Point out evidence quietly and let them find the rest.
ask: What did you see that proves your answer, or doesn't?
What did the guide point out that you'd have walked past?
steps.tip: Guides know where to look. Ask them to show you one piece of evidence on the spot, not just tell you.

levels.explore: Take three photos that help answer your why question.
levels.develop: Fill in the Field notes card, and ask the guide one question.
levels.extend: Collect evidence for your answer, and find one thing that doesn't fit.

steps.title: Explain it
steps.why: If they can explain it to someone else, they've really understood it.
steps.kid: Your kid makes My field study page at the end of the guide: the question, the guess, the answer, the evidence and how the feature shapes life here, like what grows, what lives there and where people build.
steps.you: Ask them to explain it to you first, out loud, before anything is written. Then ask 'So how does this change life for people here?'
ask: How would you explain it to a friend in one minute?
How does it change life for the people or animals here?
steps.tip: Have them explain it standing up, like a ranger at a trailhead. The words they use out loud are usually the ones to write.

levels.explore: Point to your best photo and tell a parent the answer to your question, while they write it under the photo.
levels.develop: Make the full page: question, guess, answer, evidence and one way it shapes life here.
levels.extend: Make the page, then predict how the feature will look in 100 years, and give your evidence.

conclusion.headline: They didn't just see the view. They understood it.
conclusion.text: On your next walk, stop and point at something in the land, like a cliff, a stream or a leaning tree, and ask how it got like that. Listen for a guess with a reason, then a question about how they could check it.
conclusion.celebrate: When they explain it to you, say: 'You went and checked it with your own eyes. That's what scientists do.'
extensions: Study the same kind of feature in a new place, like a second volcano or another swamp, and compare them
Find out how the feature has changed people's lives here over a hundred years
Find a feature near home and study it the same way
Map every feature you've studied on your travels, with one line on each

signs: They ask why a landscape looks the way it does
They read park signs and want to stop at visitor centres
They spot clues in the land on ordinary walks, like a dry riverbed or a bent tree
makeItReal: Before every hike from now on, ask your kid for one why question about where you're going. Write it on the map or in the notebook, and check the answer together at the top.

fromHome.text: In El Salvador we hiked the Santa Ana volcano. Before we went, the kids researched why the water at the bottom of the crater is so green, so when we looked down from the rim they knew what they were seeing. In Florida, we walked through a swamp in Jupiter with a guide, who taught us about the alligators, the water and the trees.
